summary: PCE is a key component of software-defined networking. This informational document describes an architecture in which PCE and PCEP are used in a network with central control, so a central controller can compute and update paths as the network or demand changes.

eli5.summary: One control tower decides every plane's path and can change the path when the weather changes, rather than each plane picking its own.

questions: how can pce be used for sdn
what is a pce based central controller
can pcep be used as a southbound protocol
how do pce controllers scale and stay resilient
subtitle: How a Path Computation Element can act as a central network controller, speaking PCEP straight to the routers.

tldr.problem: Software-Defined Networking needs a component that plans how traffic uses the network, but the Path Computation Element (PCE) was originally built only to hand paths to the head end of MPLS label switched paths.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes a hybrid architecture in which the PCE-based controller also speaks the PCE Communication Protocol (PCEP) as its southbound interface, so one controller and one protocol can program routers with or without a control plane.
tldr.outcome: It is an architecture and applicability document only: it defines no protocol extensions and leaves use cases and extensions to other documents.

today: RFC 8283 is an Informational RFC and, according to the metadata for this entry, has not been obsoleted or updated. Use cases and any PCEP extensions were left to other documents, such as the work-in-progress drafts it cites.

sections.title: From Path Computation to Central Control
sections.content:
The Path Computation Element (PCE) was developed to offload path computation from routers in an MPLS traffic-engineered network. Its role has since grown to cover uses such as GMPLS, delegated control and PCE-initiated use of network resources.

In Software-Defined Networking (SDN), software in a centralized controller programs the devices in the network. The RFC points out that SDN needs a component that plans how network resources are used, and that this is exactly what a PCE does. SDN is much broader than signaled MPLS networks, so the RFC argues it is reasonable to consider PCEP as a general southbound control protocol, meaning the protocol the central controller uses to talk to network elements.
sections.eli5: The tower that used to only suggest routes could be the one that runs the whole airport, and this document explains how.

sections.title: The Central Controller Architecture
sections.content:
An orchestrator, service manager, OSS or NMS asks the PCE-based controller to create connectivity. The controller computes paths using the topology, available resources and other services held in the Traffic Engineering Database (TED). It then sends a request using PCEP to a Network Element (NE), which uses a control plane to establish the connections.

The RFC contrasts three shapes. In the first, PCEP reaches one NE that signals onward. In the second, a separate network controller sits between the PCE and the NEs and uses its own southbound interface. The RFC calls this approach overly complicated, because it needs two controllers and two southbound protocols, and insufficiently flexible, because it assumes no control plane.

The third is the hybrid approach the RFC describes. The PCE-enabled controller speaks PCEP to each NE along a path, so it can work with control-plane-enabled NEs and also program individual NEs with the same protocol. The RFC says PCEP can already act as a southbound interface and needs only small, use-case-specific changes. It also notes a trade-off: a control plane can simplify deployment, for example by distributing recovery actions, or it can add operational complexity.
sections.eli5: One helper that can talk both to routers that think for themselves and to routers that just follow orders is simpler than two helpers who each speak a different language.

sections.title: Resilience and Scaling
sections.content:
A central controller can fail or become overloaded. The RFC describes three architectural mechanisms, which a deployment may combine.

  • Partitioned network: several controllers each control part of the network, called domains. This eases load but needs coordination for end-to-end connections and does not remove the single point of failure within a domain. PCEP can also be used between PCEs for this coordination.
  • Multiple parallel controllers: each controller can control every NE, so the failure of one does not leave the network unmanageable. The controllers must synchronize, which is simple for two but can be a hard problem for more. They can also be presented as a cluster that looks like one controller from outside.
  • Hierarchical controllers: a parent PCE takes a high-level view and distributes tasks to child controllers. It helps with loading and scaling and with end-to-end connectivity across domains, but does little against controller failure. The model can be recursive.

The RFC warns that a shared database used for synchronization may simply move the congestion and single point of failure somewhere else.
sections.eli5: If one tower is overloaded or breaks, you can split the sky between several towers, keep spare towers ready, or put a chief tower above them all.

sections.title: Where It Applies
sections.content:
The applicability section is deliberately brief. It does not say a PCE-based controller is mandatory or recommended, and omitting a use case does not limit applicability.

By technology it lists control-plane-operated MPLS and GMPLS networks, static LSPs in MPLS (where the controller manages part of each router's label space), MPLS multicast, transport SDN, segment routing and Service Function Chaining. By function it lists traffic engineering, traffic classification and service delivery, such as protection, VPNs and pseudowires. In each case the controller computes the answer and uses PCEP to install it.
sections.eli5: The tower could help with many jobs, such as steering traffic, sorting it into lanes and setting up special services, but this document only mentions them as ideas.

sections.title: What PCEP Needs to Change
sections.content:
PCEP is a push-pull protocol between a server (the PCE) and clients (the PCCs, which here are network elements). It already has a message, the LSP Initiate Request (PCInitiate), that a PCE sends to install state, and a response, the Path Computation State Report (PCRpt), that confirms it.

So the RFC expects only relatively minor changes: extensions to carry extra information for particular use cases, kept backward compatible and not harming existing PCEP deployments. Implementations should be able to pick a profile of extensions, and profiles should be identifiable in the protocol itself so interoperability testing can be limited. If parallel controllers are used, mechanisms for synchronizing state are also needed.
sections.eli5: The tower's radio already works well, so it only needs a few small new words added for each new job.

sections.title: Security and Manageability
sections.content:
Security is little different from any other PCE system and relies on PCEP security features and the additional mechanisms in RFC 8253. Without a control plane, the chain of trust is replaced by individual trust relationships between the controller and each NE, which may be easier to manage.

A central controller is also a central point of failure, so the network can be vulnerable to denial-of-service attacks on it, and it is a focus for interception and modification of messages to NEs. The RFC says the security implications of SDN have not been fully discussed. It also states that the architecture is itself a management architecture and that the document requires no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: With one tower in charge, everyone must trust the tower, and if someone attacks the tower, the whole airport has a problem.
